items.elicits: Chooses and executes a comparison strategy for 3/4 vs 5/8 (both fractions sit on the same side of one-half, so a bare half-split will not resolve it) and shows work supporting the symbol written.
Chooses and executes a comparison strategy for 2/3 vs 7/12 (again both above one-half) and shows work supporting the symbol written.
Chooses and executes a comparison strategy for 5/6 vs 8/9, a near-one pair, and shows work supporting the symbol written.

claims.supports: A teacher may conclude that, under proctored conditions with novel number pairs, students can select and execute a valid strategy (common denominator, benchmark, or visual model) to compare two unlike fractions and show reasoning that supports the comparison symbol they wrote.
does_not_support: Does not confirm confident use of the benchmark strategy specifically, since none of the three pairs sits on opposite sides of one-half; a student could avoid benchmark reasoning entirely and still succeed on every item.
Does not distinguish strategy quality unless the written 'how you know' work is scored alongside the symbol -- a bare correct symbol with no supporting work is close to a one-in-three guess.
Does not support comparing more than two fractions at once or ordering a set of fractions.
Is easily mistaken for evidence of G5C2core's common-denominator construction when a student happens to choose that strategy here, but the strategy is optional on these items, not required.

delegation.reason: Under direct proctoring, individual work, no AI, and paper/pencil only, the strategy choice and supporting work must happen on the page in view of the proctor.

components.component: chooses among equivalent-fraction, benchmark, or visual-model strategies
components.evidence: Instruction: 'show how you know (a common denominator, a picture, or a benchmark like 1/2)' permits any of the three named strategies.

components.component: executes the chosen strategy correctly (computation or drawing)
components.evidence: 'Show all work' plus the per-part instruction to show the method.

components.component: shows reasoning that links the work to the symbol chosen
components.evidence: 'Then show how you know' ties the justification directly to the symbol.

gate1_components.why: Every observable component the claim names -- strategy choice, execution, the symbol, and reasoning tied to the symbol -- is already exercised by items 1-3 under supervised, novel conditions. Nothing qualifies to carry forward.

gate2_materiality.why: Not reached: Gate 1 found no absent component.

gate3_value.why: Not reached: Gate 1 already failed (nothing absent to weigh).

claims.why_no_intervention: Items 1-3 jointly exercise strategy choice, execution, the symbol, and reasoning tied to the symbol -- everything the claim names -- under proctored, novel conditions. There is no absent component to repair.
claims.over_verified_note: Three items for one conceptual claim is proportionate given the varied number relationships tested (both-above-half, near-one); not excessive.

items.elicits: Constructs a common denominator (sixths) for 1/2 and 1/3, converts both, and adds the like-sized numerators.
Constructs a common denominator (twelfths) for 5/6 and 1/4, converts both, and subtracts the like-sized numerators.
Constructs a common denominator (twelfths) for the fractional parts of two mixed numbers, converts, and adds them while also managing the whole-number parts.
Constructs a common denominator (twelfths) for 3/4 and 5/6 inside a word-problem context and adds the like-sized numerators.
Constructs a common denominator (twelfths) for 2/3 and 1/4 inside a word-problem context and subtracts the like-sized numerators.

claims.supports: A teacher may conclude that students can construct a common denominator for two unlike fractions, including within mixed numbers and word-problem contexts, and correctly add or subtract the resulting like-sized parts, based on five independent, novel items.
does_not_support: Does not test denominators needing a larger or less-friendly common multiple -- every LCD used here is 6 or 12 -- so it does not speak to fluency with harder denominator pairs.

The 'compares' half of the claim is reliably exercised only if a student happens to choose the common-denominator strategy on Part A, which is optional there, not required; this instrument mainly carries the 'combines' half directly and unconditionally.
Does not support speed or automaticity beyond what fits inside the 25-minute, nine-item total.

A correct final answer on items 4-8 reflects common-denominator construction and combination specifically, not necessarily correct simplification or regrouping -- those are separate steps evaluated under G5C2a and G5C2b and can fail independently of this skill.

delegation.reason: Under proctoring with novel numbers and paper/pencil only, the common-denominator construction and the add/subtract step must be shown on the page as it happens.

components.component: finds a valid common denominator for two unlike denominators
components.evidence: All five items require unlike-denominator addition or subtraction with no shared denominator given.

components.component: converts both fractions to that common denominator
components.evidence: 'Show every step' requires the conversion to be visible.

components.component: combines (adds/subtracts) the resulting like-sized numerators correctly
compares the resulting like-sized parts using a common denominator
components.evidence: Common denominator is one of three permitted strategies in Part A, so it is available but not required there.

gate1_components.why: The claim's core (construct a common denominator, then combine) is fully and unconditionally present in items 4-8; the 'compare' alternative is also available in Part A. Nothing is absent.

gate2_materiality.why: Not reached: Gate 1 found no absent component.

gate3_value.why: Not reached: Gate 1 already failed (nothing absent to weigh).

claims.why_no_intervention: Five independent, novel items already require constructing a common denominator and combining the like-sized parts, spanning addition, subtraction, mixed numbers, and word-problem framing. Nothing named by the claim is missing.
claims.over_verified_note: Five items (4,5,6,7,8) is more coverage than a single procedural claim strictly needs; not harmful, but a teacher trimming the assessment could safely drop one of items 4/5/8 (the most similar in structure) without losing evidence for this claim.

items.elicits: Nothing toward simplification -- 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6, already in lowest terms, so no reduction step is ever required.
Nothing toward simplification -- 5/6 - 1/4 = 7/12, already in lowest terms.
Nothing toward simplification -- the fractional part of the result, 1/12, is already in lowest terms (the required step here is regrouping, not reducing).
Nothing toward simplification -- 3/4 + 5/6 = 1 7/12, and 7/12 is already in lowest terms.
Nothing toward simplification -- 2/3 - 1/4 = 5/12, already in lowest terms.

claims.supports: Nothing: no item's correct answer is a reducible fraction, so this assessment produces no evidence about whether students can simplify a result to lowest terms, despite the instruction 'Answers in simplest form.'
does_not_support: Does not distinguish a student who would forget to simplify from one who would remember to, since the step is never required for a correct answer anywhere on this assessment.

A teacher reading 'Answers in simplest form' plus all-correct scores on items 4-8 could easily read that as evidence of simplification ability -- it is not, because no computed result here is reducible.
Does not affect the separate evidence already available for G5C2core or G5C2b, which remains intact on the same items.
No guess-rate caveat applies (all items are constructed-response), but the absence itself is the caveat: a perfect score on Part B/C carries no information about this specific skill.

delegation.reason: The skill is never actually required for a correct answer on this instrument, so there is no submitted evidence on this component to delegate in the first place.

claims.gap_statement: We cannot tell from this assessment whether students can simplify a reducible fraction result to lowest terms, because none of the computed results in items 4-8 are reducible -- the 'simplest form' instruction is never actually triggered by the numbers used.

components.component: recognizes a computed fraction/mixed-number result is not in lowest terms
components.evidence: Checked each result: 1/2+1/3=5/6, 5/6-1/4=7/12, 2 1/3+1 3/4=4 1/12, 3/4+5/6=1 7/12, 2/3-1/4=5/12 -- every fractional part is already in lowest terms.

components.component: correctly reduces a reducible result to lowest terms
components.evidence: Same computation check as above; no result requires this step, so it is never demonstrated.

gate1_components.carried_forward: produces a reduced, lowest-terms answer on an item whose computed result is actually reducible
gate1_components.why: Both parts of this claim -- noticing a result needs reducing and executing the reduction -- are absent for the same reason across every computation item, and neither is assessed elsewhere in this instrument or excused by the declared conditions; the assessment's own 'simplest form' instruction shows the teacher intends to test it here.

gate2_materiality.why: The teacher's instruction 'Answers in simplest form' shows this assessment is meant to carry G5C2a, so a summative read of items 4-8 as covering this claim would draw a conclusion the evidence cannot support -- the teacher would not otherwise know the numbers never require reducing.

gate3_value.why: Repairing this costs nothing beyond adjusting one number in one existing item; the value (turning an already-declared but silently unfulfilled instruction into real evidence) clearly exceeds that near-zero burden.

modify.what_it_now_forces: The unsimplified difference is 3/6, which is reducible to 1/2; the student must now reduce to earn full credit, a step the original numbers (result 7/12) never required.

items.elicits: Converts the improper fractional sum 13/12 into 1 1/12 and combines it with the whole-number total to reach 4 1/12.
Converts the improper fractional sum 19/12 into 1 7/12, per the item's explicit instruction to write the answer as a mixed number.

claims.supports: A teacher may conclude that students can recognize when an addition result's fractional part is improper and convert it to a correctly regrouped mixed number, based on two independent, novel items.
does_not_support: Does not support regrouping/borrowing in mixed-number subtraction (e.g., borrowing a whole when the minuend's fractional part is smaller than the subtrahend's) -- no item requires it, and that is a related but distinct operation from converting an improper addition result.

Only two items exercise this component, both addition; if a student misses one for a reason upstream of regrouping (e.g., an error in finding the common denominator), the regrouping step itself can be hard to isolate at scoring.

Is adjacent to and easily conflated with G5C2a (simplifying) -- regrouping an improper fraction to a mixed number and reducing a fraction to lowest terms are different operations that scoring can blur together.

delegation.reason: Under proctoring with novel numbers and paper/pencil only, the regrouping step must be shown as part of the visible work on items 6 and 7.

components.component: recognizes an addition result's fractional part is improper (13/12 or 19/12, both >= 1)

components.component: converts the improper fractional part to whole + proper fraction and combines with any existing whole number

components.component: regroups/borrows in a mixed-number subtraction context
components.evidence: The claim's wording names an 'improper fraction result' regrouped to a mixed number, which describes an addition-side overflow; no subtraction item here uses mixed numbers or requires borrowing, and none of the five confirmed claims names this borrowing skill.

gate1_components.why: Both components the claim's own wording names -- recognizing an improper result and converting it to a mixed number -- are present in items 6 and 7. Subtraction-side borrowing is a neighbouring skill the claim's wording does not name and no confirmed claim covers; its absence does not narrow support for G5C2b as stated.

gate2_materiality.why: Not reached: Gate 1 found no qualifying absent component.

gate3_value.why: Not reached: Gate 1 already failed (nothing absent to weigh).

claims.why_no_intervention: Items 6 and 7 already require recognizing an improper fractional sum and converting it to a correctly regrouped mixed number, independently and under novel numbers. Nothing the claim's wording names is missing.

items.elicits: Locates the specific error in an unfamiliar incorrect solution (adding denominators as well as numerators) and computes the correct sum; as worded, the prompt does not require the student to state why the error produces a wrong-sized part specifically, only to 'explain what the student did wrong.'

claims.narrower_inference: Locates a specific, named error in an unfamiliar incorrect fraction-addition solution and computes the correct sum via a valid procedure.
claims.supports: A teacher may conclude that students can locate the specific error in an unfamiliar incorrect fraction-addition solution and produce the correct sum via a valid procedure.
does_not_support: As worded, does not guarantee the student states WHY the error produces a wrong-sized part (the unit-size reasoning) rather than only naming the missing procedural step, such as 'should have found a common denominator.'
Does not distinguish a student who has memorized the corrective rule from one who understands why differently-denominated pieces cannot be added directly.
Is easily mistaken for evidence of G5C2core (a correct final answer) alone, since 'show the correct answer' is part of the same item and could be scored without weighing the explanation.

Single item, single error type (adding denominators and numerators separately) -- does not generalize to diagnosing other common fraction-addition errors, such as forgetting to convert a mixed number first.

delegation.reason: Under direct supervision with a novel incorrect solution and no AI or reference access, the diagnosis and correct recomputation must happen on the page in view of the proctor.

claims.gap_statement: We cannot tell from this assessment, as item 9 is currently worded, whether students understand why adding denominators produces a wrong-sized part or have only memorized the corrective procedure, because the prompt does not require that reasoning to be stated explicitly.

components.component: locates the specific error in the shown incorrect solution
components.evidence: 'Explain what the student did wrong' directs attention to the specific error.

components.component: articulates WHY the error produces a wrong-sized part (unit-size reasoning), not just which step was skipped
components.evidence: The prompt only says 'Explain what the student did wrong' -- a minimal answer naming the missing procedure ('should have found a common denominator') satisfies this wording without ever stating why the resulting piece is the wrong size.

components.component: produces the correct sum via a valid procedure
components.evidence: 'Show the correct answer' requires the corrected computation.

gate1_components.carried_forward: articulates WHY the error produces a wrong-sized part (unit-size reasoning), not just which step was skipped
gate1_components.why: This is the only component both absent from the item's current wording and central to the claim (the claim's own phrase is 'states why... produces a wrong-sized part'); it is the sole item for this claim, so nothing elsewhere picks it up, and its absence narrows what can be concluded from a correct-looking response.

gate2_materiality.why: The claim is explicitly diagnostic ('states why'); if the item lets a purely procedural fix earn full marks, a teacher reading a correct response as evidence of conceptual understanding would be drawing a conclusion this item does not license.

gate3_value.why: The fix is a wording addition to the existing item -- no new item, no added minutes, no added grading burden -- so the value of closing a real conceptual/procedural ambiguity clearly exceeds the cost.

modify.current_text: A student added 1/2 + 1/4 and got 2/6. Explain what the student did wrong, and show the correct answer.
modify.replacement_text: A student added 1/2 + 1/4 and got 2/6. Explain why adding the denominators gives a piece that is the wrong size (not just which step was skipped), and show the correct answer.
modify.what_it_now_forces: Requires the student to name the unit-size reasoning -- why the resulting 'sixths' are not a valid consistent partition -- rather than allowing a bare procedural fix like 'should have found a common denominator' to earn full credit.

conditions_echo: Individual work, proctored in class, AI prohibited and enforced, paper and pencil only, summative, 25 minutes, end of Unit 4; the item types have been practiced but these specific numbers and problems are novel to the students.
reviewer_notes: Under these fully supervised, novel, paper-only conditions, every item on this instrument produces independent evidence when it targets a claim at all, so delegation is 'no' throughout and the interesting findings are about coverage, not authorship. G5C1, G5C2core, and G5C2b are already fully carried by the existing items -- no changes warranted. Two real, cheap gaps surfaced: G5C2a's 'simplest form' instruction is never actually triggered because every computed result on this version happens to already be in lowest terms, and item 9 (G5C3) asks students to explain the error but does not require the specific 'wrong-sized part' reasoning the claim names, so it can be satisfied by a purely procedural answer. Both are one-item, zero-cost wording/number tweaks, not new items.
